The post WEEKEND READING: HERA at 10: the providers building the future of higher education  appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Alex Proudfoot, Chief Executive of Independent Higher Education.

On 16 May 2016, a quietly revolutionary document with the name Success as a Knowledge Economy slipped out of the Government communications machine and rippled across the higher education sector. The Higher Education and Research Act that followed would transform the architecture of a system failing to keep pace with the profound changes already affecting it.

Participation had expanded, students were becoming more diverse, and specialist providers were already delivering higher education through more flexible and industry-focused routes. Funding increasingly followed students, but regulation remained rooted in an earlier world: an essentially closed group of publicly funded universities serving a predominantly young, full-time and residential population.

England needed a more open system capable of supporting innovation and recognising excellent education wherever it emerged.

One month later, a few dozen college principals and senior staff gathered in an unassuming room in a Georgian terrace on Bedford Square to reconstitute and relaunch Independent Higher Education: a powerful new identity for the voice of the independent sector at the beginning of a chapter overflowing with possibility.

The timing was no coincidence – we had spent the previous year making the case for a more open, coherent and student-centred system. The reforms promised to give high-quality independent providers a permanent place within it, although certain events towards the end of June 2016 meant that higher education wouldn’t top the political agenda for long.

Creating space for different answers

Our 2015 election manifesto called for a comprehensive framework covering public and independent providers alike: universal registration, equitable access to funding, proportionate rather than uniform regulation, stronger student protection, portable credit and support for accelerated, blended, part-time and flexible study. Rather ambitiously, we also called for a Higher Education Bill by 2017.

The Government did not simply adopt our proposals, and many others helped shape the settlement. But the same fundamental shift was clear: regulation should recognise quality rather than inherited institutional status. Ideas advanced from the margins had moved to the centre of policy.

The genius of HERA was not that it predicted exactly what the university of the future would look like, but that it created space for different answers to emerge.

A statutory Register, new routes to Degree Awarding Powers, student protection and proportionate regulation were intended to support a more diverse system. Student choice and, yes, competition were not side-effects. Innovation, new entry and academic autonomy were fundamental to HERA’s vision.

Its architects understood that, in a period of rapid change, government could not prescribe a single model for the future. But it could create the conditions in which different institutions could test different answers, and students could decide which of them best met their individual needs.

Students responded

At IHE’s Annual Conference this week, we launched State of the Sector 2026, the first report in a new annual series combining official data with our own survey evidence to track the changing scale and impact of independent higher education.

Independent providers in the public HESA data taught 76,275 students in 2018/19. By 2024/25, that figure had reached 169,805: growth of 123 per cent, compared with 13 per cent among traditional providers. UK student numbers at independent providers rose by 92 per cent, accounting for 28 per cent of all UK-domiciled growth across higher education.

But the numbers are less interesting than what those choices mean for students.

At Chickenshed, over 60 per cent of higher education students have an EHCP or disclosed disability. Teams of practitioners provide individual support without interrupting the session, while alumni mentors show students pathways into the profession. Inclusion is not added to the model, itt is an integral part of it.

At Escape Studios, animation, visual effects and games students learn inside their industry. Professionals are embedded in course design, approval and assessment, and around 100 attend the annual student showcase. Industry is present throughout the experience, not waiting outside at graduation.

At the Global Institute of Sport, students connect with an international sports industry through Global Summits from London to Melbourne and experiences such as its Live Lab at a football academy in Jamaica.

At the National Motorsport Academy, students already working in motorsport study online, start in any month and turn live workplace projects into dissertations. Some also work with NMA’s professional race team.

ASU London shows why HERA’s reform of Degree Awarding Powers mattered. Opening with its own powers allowed ASU London to recruit prospective engineers for their potential rather than their Level 3 Maths grade, providing the theoretical and Mathematical support they need while solving real-world problems. Its first cohort was 50 per cent female.

These are not five versions of the traditional university but five very different ideas of what it means to be a higher education student.

That is meaningful student choice: not simply choosing between institutions, but choosing between genuinely different experiences of learning and alternative career pathways.

What they have in common is education designed around the lives and ambitions of their students, often embedded in a profession or industry and bringing academic learning, practical experience and personal development closer together.

Ambition into reality

Our report shows that these five institutions are vivid examples of a much wider pattern.

First, independent providers reach students still too often treated as peripheral to the system. Nearly two-thirds of undergraduates at independent providers are mature, almost a third come from England’s most deprived areas and 58 per cent live at home while studying. Student choice is not simply about which campus an 18-year-old moves to. For many people, it is whether higher education can fit around employment, family, geographical ties and an already complicated life.

Second, they are delivering the flexibility policymakers repeatedly say they want. Independent providers account for 96 per cent of the growth in part-time higher education since 2018/19. Eight in ten offer flexible study, and almost half intend to deliver modules through the Lifelong Learning Entitlement.

Third, ambition is turning into action. Among providers responding to our survey in both 2025 and 2026, eight in ten now offer a qualification or mode of study they did not report a year earlier. Modular provision has doubled, while 86 per cent of providers partner with employers.

Independent providers are not waiting for the future of higher education to arrive. They are building it.

Their growth is about more than numbers. It is about young people immersing themselves in subjects they love, adults returning to education or changing direction, and professionals acquiring skills that help industries innovate. What connects them is purposeful learning and the opportunity to put theory into practice.

The promise still incomplete

HERA’s potential is becoming reality, but the system has not made it easy. Three-quarters of providers say their regulatory burden has increased over the past three years. None say it has fallen. Those working through university partnerships can experience regulation twice: directly and through requirements passed down by their partner.

Innovation was supposed to be in the DNA of the Office for Students. It must have been a recessive gene, because it certainly skipped a few generations.

New entrants were deprioritised, independent providers misunderstood and regulation allowed to ossify around the assumption that one size could fit all. Registration and Degree Awarding Powers were paused, leaving providers spending eye-watering sums extending validation agreements rather than investing in students and new provision.

This is not a case for weaker regulation, but for regulation that protects students while enabling responsible growth, innovation and flexibility. Delay and uncertainty can close opportunities just as surely as poor provision can harm them.

The impressively collaborative approach of the new OfS leadership offers an opportunity to recover HERA’s original ambition. Having been at the heart of the original reforms, they understand that ambition better than most. I have confidence that they will meet the moment.

Government should see independent providers as willing and agile partners in growth, not exceptions to a university-shaped rulebook. Their contribution is already substantial. Policy should enable them to do more.

The only constant is change

In 2016, the White Paper and the legislation it inspired were needed because higher education had changed while its architecture remained rooted in the past. In 2026, HERA’s spirit must be recaptured because the sector faces what could be its greatest challenge yet – and one that only radical change may help it overcome.

For decades now the threat of technology breaching the fortified towers of higher education and unravelling its value proposition has been ringing in our ears. Personal computers. The internet. MOOCs. In 2013, Michael Barber, who would later become the first Chair of OfS, famously warned that ‘an avalanche was coming’. But then the avalanche never seemed to arrive.

Technology was transforming almost every other part of our lives, but the traditional tertiary pathway proved remarkably sticky: leave school at 18, go to university, study for three years, and then secure a graduate job. We have heard predictions of disruption so often that perhaps we have become like the villagers in the story of the boy who cried wolf.

But AI may be the wolf

Young people now expect instant access to what feels like all the knowledge in the world, explained and personalised to them in seconds. If higher education is no longer the gatekeeper of knowledge, its value must increasingly lie in what our students do with it: the problems they solve, the judgements they make, the people they learn alongside, and the capabilities they develop.

I do not pretend to know exactly what that means for universities in ten or twenty years and I am instinctively suspicious of anyone who says they do, but the answer is not that it means nothing.

Longer working lives and rapidly changing industries also make education concentrated at the beginning of adulthood increasingly inadequate to the task at hand. We need progression at 18, 28, 38 and 58. The current Government’s post-16 reforms and the Lifelong Learning Entitlement point towards a more flexible, specialised and comprehensive system of lifelong higher learning.

HERA was not the beginning or the end of that story. But ten years after the White Paper, it remains one of its most important chapters. Its spirit was confidence in the agency of students, belief in the value of diversity, and trust in the capacity of new institutions to produce new and sometimes better answers to the questions that we all face.

Today the world in which higher education takes place is changing once again. This time, regulation cannot be the last part of the system to notice.

title: Student Success and Public Trust
summary:
Student Success and Public Trust
sara.custer@in… Fri, 11/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

The people closest to struggling students may be higher ed’s best trust-building asset—but they can’t do it alone.

Byline(s)
Sara Custer
full_text:
The wisdom of crisis communications says: “If you’re explaining, you’re losing.” In the crisis of lost public trust in higher ed, too many institutions are explaining. Colleges defend their value with broad claims about lifetime earnings and graduate success. By offering counterpoints to critics, they validate the claims that college isn’t worthwhile, and their defenses fall flat with the millions of stopped out students for whom higher ed’s promises were broken. Instead of attempts to “change the narrative,” colleges need to prove that higher education is worth students’ time and money. Student success initiatives are perhaps the strongest piece of evidence colleges have to show they care about students’ futures.

At Inside Higher Ed’s annual Student Success US conference in Salt Lake City this week, a few things became apparent: Student success leaders clearly see students’ unique needs and learning goals. These administrators are not shy about naming higher ed’s failures to support students. They own those shortcomings and, despite thin staffing and minimal funds, their departments persist in coming up with new ways to address them.

The student success leaders in Utah told hard truths. They acknowledged that many of their institutions aren’t designed with students’ needs in mind—support services are only available from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; disjointed points of service have students running laps around campus, from the bursar to the financial aid office, to get answers to urgent questions. Institutions send too many emails, issue too many surveys and don’t use data effectively, administrators said. Faculty are often not included in student success conversations, they observed. Leaders grieved the students who drop out after the first semester when they can’t pay their first tuition bill.

But at the event, these admissions came paired with solutions, however small. The director of basic needs at a large public university found that 90 percent of students who received emergency aid enrolled in the next semester. Of those who got no aid, just 20 percent persisted. Committed to keeping more students enrolled, she launched a fundraising campaign specifically for emergency funds.

This is one example of how institutions are trying to support students with interventions. Others target food insecurity and meeting students’ housing and childcare needs. Complete College America (CCA) this week published a basic needs support guide for the growing number of institutions—from community colleges to large research universities— developing these programs. Meeting students’ basic needs is “the next frontier of the completion agenda,” Yolanda Watson Spiva, president of CCA, said in a release about the report. “Successfully addressing these needs ensures that students with increasingly diverse ages, work experiences and family responsibilities can find a path to and through college.”

Basic needs interventions are just one way student success administrators are helping students get through college. Others described their tactics for untangling institutional bureaucracies for students. When the University of Utah, our event host, identified gaps in how students navigate campus services, its student success leaders worked with students and staff to develop Answer U, a student support system that connects learners to career coaching, financial aid and scholarships, and academic advising. Mitzi Montoya, the university’s provost and executive vice president for academic affairs, said the system saves students from going from office to office to get information. Students’ questions also give her team real-time information on what they’re struggling with. “[We] understand where we need to redesign systems and processes because the answers are not easy to find,” she said at the conference. “And we now have a whole series of other projects related to it.”

Administrators also recognized that support services must adapt to students’ unique needs and learning goals. Academic advising for an 18-year-old is different from what a returning adult student needs, for example. And while lawmakers might equate higher ed’s value with graduate jobs and salaries, data from 55,000 students in the National Survey of Student Engagement’s (NSSE) Career & Workforce Module undercuts those assumptions. Students ranked expected job salary and availability fourth among the items that influence their career plans. Both first year and senior students said the factors that influence their career plans more are: Finding a job that fits their interests and abilities; a desire to make a difference in their community; and wanting to make an impact on society. Jillian Kinzie, associate director of the Indiana University Center for Postsecondary Research and the NSSE Institute, said the findings are a “serious” indication that students’ career goals are driven by their passions and desire to make a difference. “Two things to keep top of mind [for higher ed institutions] are: What are students looking for? And then, how are we going to communicate our larger responsibility to ensure employment and earnings together?” Kinzie told administrators.

Despite the initiatives and energy on display this week, student success can only go so far. Many of the problems contributing to America’s declining opinion about higher education require more systemic change. Colleges and universities are still perceived as too expensive and too many institutions are not transparent about cost. In our recent Student Voice survey of more than 5,000 students, just a quarter were highly confident their college or university is taking meaningful steps toward affordability, such as reducing unnecessary costs, limiting tuition increases or pooling resources. And just 29 percent fully grasp the total cost of attendance, beyond tuition. Student success leaders can’t communicate the impact of academic research or protect the public funding needed to sustain it, either. And while they can create mentoring programs to help students maintain academic momentum and provide teaching and learning training to faculty, student success leaders can’t change academic incentive structures that reward research over teaching, or control whether a curriculum is relevant to employers.

A first step to rebuild trust in higher education is admitting that too many students fall through the cracks—a reality the student success leaders readily acknowledged in Utah this week. As those administrators return to their campuses with new ideas and renewed energy for their work, I hope they have the full support of their institutions. Student success leaders can spearhead initiatives that show a skeptical public that colleges want their students to thrive, but they can’t do it alone.

title: New Rule Changes the Future of Programmatic Accreditation
summary:
New Rule Changes the Future of Programmatic Accreditation
jessica.blake@… Fri, 11/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

Policy experts largely agree trade groups have too much influence over certain accreditors, driving up the time and money students spend on higher education. But not all believe Trump’s new regulations will ease the antitrust concerns.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
For years, Republican policymakers have been concerned about what some describe as a “cozy relationship” between accreditors and the trade groups they represent, arguing that it creates a glaring conflict of interest that breeds unnecessary evaluation standards, credential inflation and higher college costs.

Now, as the Trump administration implements new federal regulations and tries to crack down on what it alleges are antitrust violations, experts say certain accreditors could face significant changes. Some agencies are already planning to formally end their scrutinized partnerships in order to comply with the new rule, which takes effect in July.

Earlier this month, the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) and its related accrediting body—the AVMA Council on Education—announced plans to become fully separate entities; the Association of Theological Schools is also planning to separate from its accrediting arm, the Commission on Accrediting.

Such quality assurance agencies, known as programmatic accreditors, can help specific types of degree programs—as opposed to entire institutions—access federal student aid and other government grants. But they must meet regulatory standards and be federally recognized in order to do so. Over the years, many programmatic accreditors have also become pivotal in the state licensure process for their given profession. (Students often just have to graduate from a program accredited by a specific agency to qualify for a license, but in some cases the agency also has to be federally recognized.)

For the colleges and accreditors that do require federal recognition to access aid or licensure, the new regulations effectively raise the bar they have to clear to prove “separation and independence” from any related trade groups.

This means that if programmatic agencies want to stay in ED’s good graces, they will no longer be able to depend on the larger, better-resourced professional associations for funding, staff, technology or office space. Nor will they be allowed to accept association members as volunteers on the committees that vote to determine their accreditation standards.

The separate and independent changes also apply to institutional accreditors, which comprehensively evaluate colleges and universities, but those agencies likely won’t have to make as many changes to prove they are independent.

One programmatic agency heavily targeted by the rule change is the American Bar Association’s Council of the Section of Legal Education and Admissions, which Trump’s executive order directly called on to “reform accreditation.” It was also sharply criticized at a recent Education Department panel. Many higher education experts argue the Council works too closely with ABA’s governing board, but the Trump administration has also targeted ABA for culture war issues, including its diversity equity and inclusion standards. So far, the ABA has made a few changes to its accreditation standards, but has not publicly announced any plans to restructure along the lines of AVMA or ATS.

And while both conservative and liberal consumer protection advocates largely agree that ABA and the programmatic accrediting system in general is crawling with antitrust violations, some on the left worry that the Trump administration’s approach to addressing this issue has become overly politicized and won’t be as effective as originally hoped. The rule will force many agencies to reshape their infrastructure or opt out of federal recognition, experts said, but it’s unclear if those changes will truly end the trade group’s influence on accreditation.

“Like what a lot of the Trump administration does, there is a kernel of a good idea buried under a mountain of bad policy here,” said Jeremy Bauer-Wolf, the higher education investigations manager at New America, a left-leaning think tank.

“The idea that there is too much collusion, as the administration puts it, or too much overlap between industry and accreditors is a very real and valid criticism,” Bauer-Wolf added. “But my question becomes: Do you want your posture to be, meet these very specific and sometimes overbearing rules or exit the system? I don’t know if that’s the proper posture.”

‘Consequential Decisions’

No veterinary schools depend on the AVMA’s Council on Education for access to student loans as they are all housed at larger universities with an institutional accreditor that serves as the link. But they do depend on the programmatic agency for access to certain research grants and loan repayment programs. And currently, 49 of the 62 veterinary licensure boards in the U.S. and Canada mention AVMA accreditation and/or federal recognition in their statutes.

These dependencies appear to be a driving factor behind why AVMA and the Council are parting ways, according to a news release that explains the separation, although AVMA also warns that doing so will likely be a costly endeavor.

Currently, AVMA subsidizes about 50 percent of the Council’s accreditation expenses. Under the new rule, that subsidy will no longer be possible, and colleges will have to bear the burden and other new overhead costs through their accreditation dues.

Inside Higher Ed reached out to AVMA for comment but the association declined, saying the new regulations “and their interpretation are still developing.” The group said it could say more after the Education Department releases its Accreditation Handbook “in early 2027.”

Emma Read, CEO of the American Association of Veterinary Medical Colleges, which has also served as a key partner for the AVMA Council on Education, noted that the loss of trade association members voting on accreditation standards will result in a lack of expertise. That absence of insight, she said, could lead to lower quality education and greater logistical challenges for the institutions implementing new policies.

“Who better to understand what it will mean to put a standard in place than the people that actually have to put the standard in place?” Read said. “But we recognize that the department has decided against that. So while our faculty and staff will put ideas forward and propose standard changes … we recognize we won’t have any part in that decision-making.”

Zach Waymer, executive director of the Association of Specialized and Professional Accreditors (ASPA), the association that represents programmatic accreditors, said he’s particularly concerned about the “extremely constrained timeframe” agencies have been given to make those decisions; he is not convinced the rushed implementation of new regulations will have Trump’s desired effect in squashing trade groups’ influence. The rule was finalized in late October.

“These are consequential decisions with financial, operational, and potential legal implications that take time and cost money,” Waymer said.

By sharing resources with trade associations, accreditors have been able to keep costs down and stay “at the forefront of expertise from the field,” he added. It didn’t mean that the trade group itself was making decisions for the accreditor.

“These are time and costs that spill over into programs, institutions, and even, indirectly, students,” he said. “The Department hasn’t demonstrated how these changes will improve educational quality or student outcomes.”

Impact ‘Hard to Gauge’

Not all of the roughly 30 programmatic accreditors currently recognized by the Education Department have decided to formally turn their existing accreditation arms into a new nonprofit like AVMA or ATS. At least seven have opted to withdraw from federal recognition, citing issues with the new accreditation rules.

One, the Council on Chiropractic Education, explained in an FAQ that it withdrew because Trump’s new rule included “excessively burdensome and unnecessary standards” and “weakened the peer-review process.”

Critics of Trump’s policy are most worried about these groups. When an accreditor withdraws, the federal government loses its ability to hold the accreditor accountable. But sacrificing federal recognition doesn’t prevent an accreditor from evaluating colleges for other purposes, like state licensure eligibility.

“The real impact of those changes over time is a little hard to gauge at the moment, and it’s going to depend on whether or not these agencies remain in federal recognition,” said Antoinette Flores, vice president of federal policy at the Council for Higher Education Accreditation. “I think there's an open question about whether or not making an accrediting agency be in a different building than a trade association is going to stop credential inflation and other problems we are seeing, particularly if agencies are pulling out of federal recognition altogether.”

Still, conservatives and the Trump administration have held fast to the argument that trade groups have an “outsized and direct influence” on accreditors’ decisions, which has to be addressed. They highlight AVMA as a prime example.

In 2025, the Department of Justice backed Lincoln Memorial University and its vet school in an antitrust lawsuit against AVMA. LMU took issue with the accreditation council’s requirement that institutions “maintain substantial research activities,” which are costly. The university argued in the suit that by setting this standard, the association was seeking to “make veterinary medicine a more profitable endeavor.” The lawsuit was eventually dismissed, but the DOJ argued that professional associations that “promulgate” and “enforce” accreditation standards are not exempt from antitrust laws.

“By imposing exclusionary restrictions, accreditors and occupational and professional licensors can artificially limit the supply of service providers, thus reducing output, competition, and incentives for innovation,” the department said. “This ultimately harms consumers, who face higher costs and fewer choices in service providers.”

Diane Auer Jones, a long-time critic of programmatic accreditors who served in the Education Department under both George W. Bush and the first Trump administration, added that the partnership between agencies and trade groups wasn’t always a problem. But now that they’ve transformed from voluntary systems of peer-review to “gatekeepers” who can prevent access to state licenses, professional associations have too much control.

Ideally, Auer Jones would like to see the Education Department strip programmatic accreditors of federal recognition altogether.

“Institutional accrediting agencies cannot be permitted to hold monopolies over entry to entire occupations or fields,” she said. Ending federal recognition across the board would require accreditors “to work with states and reopen multiple pathways to licensure eligibility,” which is “the most important next step the Secretary must take.”

title: Education Department faces management challenges from recent changes, watchdog says
summary: An annual federal report cited interagency agreements and a handful of executive orders as key factors that will challenge the agency in 2027.
full_text:
Dive Brief:

The U.S. Department of Education will face challenges in 2027 stemming from recent efforts to wind down the agency, according to a report from the agency's Office of Inspector General. The annual report is meant to flag the "most serious management and performance challenges the Department faces," how it’s addressing those issues, and what more it could do.

The report says the Education Department will continue to face challenges related to change management and the oversight and monitoring of funding recipients next year — specifically as a result of changes like interagency agreements, waivers from federal spending and accountability requirements under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, and layoffs that gutted the agency in 2025.

The report cited a handful of President Donald Trump's executive orders — including one signed in March 2025 directing U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon to take steps to close the federal agency and give greater authority to states — as impetus behind management challenges the department is facing.

Dive Insight:

Since early 2025, the second Trump administration has outsourced many of the Education Department’s core functions such as grant management, monitoring and technical assistance to other agencies through interagency agreements. The department has also reorganized many of its offices and laid off a bulk of its staff.

"Change of this magnitude can result in challenges associated with employee resistance, fatigue, and uncertainty — such as decreased productivity, operational disruption, and lost efficiency — and have an impact on the organization’s ability to respond to stakeholder questions and concerns," the Nov. 13 report from OIG stated.

The Education Department has not yet issued an annual performance plan for fiscal year 2026 and has yet to issue its annual performance report for FY 2025, strategic plan for FY 2026-2030, or annual performance plan for FY 2027, according to the report.

Other reports through various federal offices have flagged similar concerns with the Education Department's output amid McMahon's efforts to close the agency, which ultimately requires Congressional approval.

In June, another OIG report found that layoffs at the Education Department appear to have impacted units that wereperforming legal duties.

The staffing changes were made to 16 of the department's 17 offices, resulting in an overall reduction of at least 40% of the more than 4,000 employees who were working for the Education Department when Trump reentered office in January 2025.

Many lawmakers, civil rights groups and lawyers have raised concerns with output from at least one of those offices, the Office for Civil Rights, which saw a slowdown in case resolutions that included no sexual harassment or assault cases being settled in 2025. A later report from the office of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., showed that OCR resolved only 1% of its cases overall in 2025, the lowest percentage from any OCR in over the last decade.

Responding to a draft of the most recent OIG report, the Education Department said it had made progress in many of the areas of concern, including change management. According to OIG, the department said it has "continued efforts to improve operational processes and maintain program delivery during a period of substantial organizational change." Additionally, the agency said it has "engaged in contractor support to assist with resolution for external audits," among other adjustments.

The department has previously maintained that its staffing and organizational changes will not affect the statutory functions it is legally obliged to perform.

The department also stressed in a comment to K-12 Dive that the OIG report is an annual update. In a January OIG report, the office flagged similar oversight challenges stemming from executive orders and resulting organizational changes.

"It is critical that the Department strategically plan for and effectively manage these and other major operational changes that it may decide to undertake," it warned at the time.

full_text:
The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.

But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.

McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.

Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.

“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”

On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.

Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.

Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

title: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals
summary:
The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns

Continue reading...
full_text:
The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.

This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.

Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.

“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.

Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.

Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.

Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.

The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.

“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.

This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.

Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.

But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.

If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.

Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

title: “A one-year decline is not a one-year problem”: America’s shrinking talent pipeline
summary:
Further drops in America’s international student population are set to cost the US economy $2.4bn in lost revenue this year, with analysts warning of the long-term consequences of a shrinking pipeline of international talent.

The post “A one-year decline is not a one-year problem”: America’s shrinking talent pipeline appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The economic impact projections from NAFSA and JB International draw on fresh data from IIE’s Fall Snapshot survey revealing a 15% drop in new international students this semester – marking the third consecutive year of declining new enrolments.

In a webinar this week unpacking the trends behind the data, experts pointed squarely at policy challenges under the second Trump administration driving the downturn.

“Two years into the current Trump administration and we are really seeing the effects of what started in January 2025,” said NAFSA senior director, public policy and legislative strategy, Rachel Banks.

“In the fall of 2025, the decline wasn’t as significant as what we had feared given the unprecedented volume of visa revocations and the visa interview pause for three and a half weeks during peak visa application season,” said Banks.

“Fast forward another academic year, we’re continuing to see significant declines and it’s really hard to ignore what’s happening policy wise.”

In particular, Banks highlighted ongoing barriers to visa processing – a challenge cited by nearly nine in 10 institutions as a cause of enrolment declines in IIE’s Fall Snapshot survey.

She said that for the second consecutive year the administration had failed to prioritise student and exchange visitor visa processing during peak visa season, while the administration’s expanded travel ban continues to bar prospective students from nearly 40 nations.

Unlike during Trump’s first administration, students and exchange visitors are not exempt from the current ban, which includes Iran – a traditional sender of postgraduate students – and Nigeria, which had been rising as an important source of talent.

But counter to the unrelenting stream of negative sector news since Trump returned to office, Boston College professor Chris Glass noted said student demand remained.

“Instititutions are clear: the obstacle is access, not demand,” Glass told The PIE News.

“Among those reporting declines, 88% cite the visa process and 70% cite travel restrictions. Fewer cite competition from other countries or cost. The top reasons are barriers to entry, not loss of interest,” he said, referring to IIE’s survey data.

Optional Practical Training

Alongside a 15% fall in new students this semester, IIE’s Open Doors data for 2025/26 found international enrolments excluding OPT were down 8% on the previous year.

A 14% rise in OPT participants in 2025/26 – who are included in official student totals – meant overall student numbers dropped by 32,000 last year, resulting in an overall 3% decline.

But the latest figures showed a 6% OPT drop this fall, suggesting “the turn has started” after last year’s peak, according to Glass.

As a result, he said employers would lose early-career STEM workers while universities “lose part of what a US master’s degree attractive,” with 95% of institutions indicating students would look to other countries if the work stream were eliminated.

As such, the data is increasingly reflecting the barrage of attacks from the Trump administration on US colleges since the start of his second term, including repeated threats of fresh OPT and H-1B fees.

We are really seeing the effects of what started in January 2025

Rachel Banks, NAFSA

Currently, it is considering a $70,000 charge on universities for each OPT recommendation, which, if finalised, will make this year’s 6% drop look “small”, said Glass.

Such policies would disproportionately impact India’s student cohort, 54% of whom are graduates working on OPT, the Open Doors data revealed.

Therefore, while India leads the count on raw numbers, China is again the largest sender with approximately 193,000 enrolled students in 2024/25.

Economic impact

Presidents’ Alliance deputy director of federal policy Zuzana Cepla Wootson said the continued declines were a “serious warning sign” of growing uncertainty. She highlighted barriers at every stage of the international student journey from visa application to postgraduate work opportunities.

Notably, new analysis from the Presidents’ Alliance has revealed that while the total number of international students in the US fell by just 0.3% during Trump’s first administration, so far in his second term levels have plummeted by 6.7% from October 2024 to the same month this year.

And the trends are having a knock on impact on international students’ financial contributions. Alongside the $2.6bn, forecasts predict a loss of 31,000 jobs this year, with stakeholders highlighting the detrimental impact on domestic students and American communities.

“All Americans will feel the effects as international students’ tuition payments, local spending, and contributions to US excellence in research and innovation diminish,” said Aw.

The findings from NAFSA and JB International showed international students contributed $39.9bn to the US economy and supported 309,000 jobs in 2025-26, a 7% decline in spending and loss of more than 46,000 jobs compared to the previous academic year.

This marks the second year of decline following three years of growth and a peak of $43.8bn in economic contributions by international students in 2023-24.

Notably, the decline in economic contributions is driven not only by falling international students, but is also impacted by how different students fund their time in the US, JB International founder Jason Baumgartner explained.

While most undergraduate students are paying their own way, the proportion of international students on OPT has risen in recent years, who now make up 29% of the total, meaning a growing proportion of international students not contributing to tuition, housing or dining revenue on campuses.

Victories amid ongoing headwinds

In spite of the sobering data, Banks welcomed this week’s “tremendous litigation victory” as a federal judge vacated the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s controversial final rule to end Duration of Status, preserving the longstanding system that allows international students to remain in the US for the duration of their studies.

It comes as new data from Common App showed a surprising rebound in international applications to US colleges, up 9% compared to this time last year, as education platform Studyportals also recorded a boost in US demand following the Democrats’ sweeping mid-term election victories.

Meanwhile, the sector welcomed another court judgement this week blocking DHS efforts to dramatically limit Curricular Practical Training (CPT) opportunities for international students taking internships as part of their studies.

But Banks warned uncertainty around duration of status had already taken its toll on this year’s numbers and highlighted sustained headwinds including the proposed $70,000 OPT fee – something experts warned would “decimate” the international talent pipeline.

Long-term repercussions

Among growing warnings about America’s shrinking talent pipeline, Glass predicted repercussions would be felt “at least through the end of the decade”, with new enrollments falling by 18% last year and 15% this year.

And while there’s most volatility in one to two year graduate programs in which student numbers declined by 15% last year, he warned OPT could fall by a third by 2028 even if new enrolment stabilises.

“A one year decline is not a one year problem,” Aw told webinar delegates, urging institutions to diversify recruitment and focus on emerging countries such as Vietnam that experienced gains last year.

“The consequences can last well beyond one academic year,” added Wootson, warning of the losses for business, entrepreneurship and innovation, and the compound impact on campuses, local economies, and wider US workforce.

title: Higher Ed Security Requires Shared Responsibility for Incident Response
summary:
Like many areas of higher education, campus security has changed dramatically over time. The systems that help protect people, places and assets increasingly depend on one another. 
Physical safety technologies rely on digital infrastructure, data analytics and real-time communications. Developing a holistic plan to secure and protect the institution can take different forms — physical, digital or both — but plans, funding and responses now need to be coordinated. That means locking doors, managing identities and preparing networks and storage to handle the cameras, sensors and other…
full_text:
Today’s threats do not respect those boundaries, nor do the tools required to manage them. Mitigating risks and securing institutions require integrated technologies and coordinated efforts across departmental lines. These collaborations are critical, especially when departments have different assumptions about what an incident might mean for them. An incident can disrupt an institution in ways that are difficult to predict, which is why engaging leaders across campus is vital.

Each department brings its unique perspective to the table during an incident, so instead of asking, “Whose lane is this?” we should ask, “What happened, who is affected, and how do we respond together?” Here’s how to approach this mindset.

Establish Shared Governance for Campus Security and Incident Response

A holistic approach to campus security starts at the top. Senior leadership should set the expectation that safety and security is a shared institutional responsibility and create the governance structure accordingly.

From there, the right people need to be in the room. Who is on that list depends on the institution, but it should generally include representatives from every area that could be impacted by a security incident. Areas involved often include those responsible for the people, and physical and intellectual property of the institution, such as IT, public safety, facilities, student affairs, HR, academic affairs, marketing and communications, legal, finance and risk.

DISCOVER: An integrated physical security strategy can transform campus safety.

Members should understand their roles, the boundaries of their authority and what risk thresholds call for a particular level of response. Roles and responsibilities should be established long before an incident occurs; an emergency should not be the first time these issues are addressed.

Fragmented communication can lead to conflicting, incorrect or incomplete guidance. The goal of establishing a holistic governance structure is to create a response that is coordinated and addresses the institution as a whole. Good governance helps teams share information, make informed decisions and communicate consistently.

Security Assessments Help Campus Teams Identify Vulnerabilities

Before deciding what products to buy, policies to implement or procedures to change, an institution needs to understand its current position, which can be determined using a security assessment. A useful assessment begins with fundamental questions: Who and what do we need to protect? What threats are we aware of? What tools and skills do we have to prevent, detect and respond to threats; mitigate the risk stemming from those threats; and recover from any incident that an institution may face?

Again, bringing all parties to the table at this point in the process can only benefit the outcome. Different teams will bring their areas of expertise to the assessment, shedding light into potential threats that impact them as well as the capabilities they can offer. No one department has the full picture.

READ MORE: A physical security assessment can help higher ed leaders make AI investments.

The threats themselves are not always within an institution’s control. But through its capabilities, policies and investments, an institution can ensure it is as prepared as possible. An assessment helps identify where the readiness gaps are and what could be put in place to reduce risk. That could mean a technology investment, a policy change or a clearer process.

Incident Response Plans Require Documentation and Regular Testing

In cybersecurity, we often speak about the importance of a well-practiced incident response plan — a playbook for what to do in the event of a cybersecurity incident. This same principle applies to campus safety threats.

Start with a clear outline of what needs to happen at a high level, then add detailed sections for the teams responsible for each part of the response. Participants should be able to understand their roles long before an incident occurs.

Rehearsing the plan is just as important as having one. Tabletop scenarios should challenge the incident response team with complicated situations, not just straightforward ones. Bringing in a third party can help teams run the exercise to test each party’s readiness, particularly when multiple departments, stakeholders and systems are involved.

Institutions should also test the tools and processes they rely on. Emergency alerts, building systems and other critical capabilities need regular checks to ensure they are functioning properly. Practice can also include short, small and controlled group exercises with unannounced process drills on an ad hoc basis to test key team members’ readiness.

EXPLORE: Real-time security centers continually monitor campus environments.

Readiness comes from repetition and refinement. The goal of these tests and run-throughs is to learn where the incident response plan works and what needs to improve.

Implement Shared Responsibility for Higher Ed Security

If your teams are not talking regularly, start by reaching across departments. Ask colleagues outside of the IT department whether they understand their role in the institution’s security responsibilities and incident response plans. Identify the gaps you find, then bring them to executive leadership or a representative who can raise them to those on top. Come equipped with options for addressing these gaps, including some of the strategies mentioned here.

Organizations do not have to solve every issue at once, but they do need to start building the relationships, governance and shared understanding that make coordinated action possible. Partners such as CDW can help institutions assess where they are, identify gaps, develop governance materials and consider ways to strengthen physical and digital security capabilities. We have relationships with vendors across categories, so we know how the physical and digital tools work together and what policies and procedures institutions should have in place to ensure every base is covered.

Campus security is not only about technology systems, buildings and departments. It is also about protecting people and the university’s mission, no matter the type of threat. That work is most effective when the institution approaches it as a shared responsibility.

title: Taking an arts-based path when doing research in or on higher education contexts: inside perspectives from newer researchers
summary: by Tim Clark, Charlie Davis and Kathleen Pithouse-Morgan Over the next few weeks we’re delighted to be able to share this collection of blog posts by newer researchers using arts-based educational research (ABER). Work discussed in this series is grounded … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Tim Clark, Charlie Davis and Kathleen Pithouse-Morgan

Over the next few weeks we’re delighted to be able to share this collection of blog posts by newer researchers using arts-based educational research (ABER). Work discussed in this series is grounded in the respective authors’ experiences either researching higher education (HE) or developing as researchers in an HE context. There are five posts in total: one from us the editing authors and four from newer researchers at different stages of their careers. The posts are intended for both newer researchers and people responsible for teaching ABER or supervising others embracing its creative possibilities.

The series aims to prompt readers to consider how they might use ABER approaches in their own work. We hope to do this through the authors’ experiences of using ABER. Individually, they illustrate how ABER draws on creative ways of thinking and working to explore educational questions and communicate research findings. There are discussions about poetry, storytelling, crafting, messy map making and more.

Contributions to this blog series reflect a growing interest in using creative research methods to understand higher education policy and practice (Brooke et al, 2024; Flint & Toledo, 2021). Researchers have used poetry (Pithouse-Morgan & Le, 2026), storyboards (Illingworth et al, 2025), collage (James et al, 2025) and meme-making (Tidy et al, 2024) to explore a wide range of issues, practices and challenges. Yet newer researchers may feel apprehensive about using these approaches, including how their work will be understood or evaluated (Clark & Dobson, 2025).

The beginnings of this special issue can be traced to a conversation during a break at the 2025 SRHE Conference, when we started talking about newer researchers’ growing interest in creative methods. We carried the conversation into an online SRHE Newer Researchers Network workshop, inviting participants to explore object work, poetry, poetic making and storyboarding. The workshop, which first ran in July 2026 and will return on 4 March 2027, became a lively space for making, sharing and discussion. The interest it generated prompted us to think about how we could share more examples and offer further opportunities to encounter this work. Those conversations continued after the workshop and led to this blog series.

As we developed the workshop and this collection, we reflected together on our own routes into arts-based research and the people and communities that supported us. Our conversation turned to how arts-based research might become more visible and accessible to newer researchers, rather than something they might encounter only by chance. We invite you to join the conversation and consider what ABER might offer as you conduct research within or about higher education.

Encountering arts-based research

Kathleen Pithouse-Morgan: For me, it was meeting Claudia Mitchell when I was a doctoral student that started me on the arts-based research path. That worked out well for me, but access to creative approaches shouldn’t depend on serendipity or on meeting the right person at the right time. It should be more integrated into doctoral and early career academic development so nobody misses out.

Newer researchers often turn to handbooks and textbooks, as well as university-based classes and seminars, for ideas about what research can be and how they might approach it. Yet, when they attend wider academic seminars and conferences, people often say, “Nobody in our university department is talking about this,” or ask, “Where do we go to hear about this?” Whether someone encounters creative research can depend on its visibility in their immediate academic setting.

Charlie Davis: It is often about visibility. Long-established ideas about what research is and what it should look like affect how we understand researchers and who we recognise as a researcher. One contributor to this special issue talked about never having connected her making activities with research. Making this work visible shows that people are doing it and have been doing it for a long time. It opens up possibilities beyond persistent representations of research and researchers being limited to a narrow range of practices.

Tim Clark: There is something important about permission, being part of a community and seeing that other people are working in these ways. Another contributor described her surprise when she discovered that it was possible to research in this way. She saw an example and thought, “I could actually do my research that way. I didn’t think that would be accepted or meet the requirements.” Sharing examples helps people see the range of approaches available within higher education research.

Finding a supportive community

Kathleen Pithouse-Morgan: When newer researchers share unfinished work, it helps doctoral students and early career academics see something within their reach. If they encounter only highly accomplished work produced by people with a great deal of experience, it can seem unattainable. Work at an intermediate stage can encourage someone to think, “I could do that.” Sharing unfinished work helps both the person receiving feedback and the people who encounter it.

Tim Clark: That is why it matters to include doctoral students and early career researchers directly in the blog. It connects with the purpose of SRHE and the Newer Researchers Network. The collection creates a space where readers can browse different contributions and encounter work that sits at a different stage than more finished examples.

There is a useful connection between the SRHE conference and this collection. At the conference, you might hear a professor speak and then a doctoral student discuss work in progress. The blog can bring voices from doctoral and early career researchers alongside those of more established academics.

Charlie Davis: In my experience, the SRHE has been an inclusive space where people at the beginning of their careers are valued for their contributions. At conferences, there is a clear effort to help doctoral students and early career researchers feel comfortable sharing their work.

The SRHE Newer Researchers Network gives people opportunities to share work that is unfinished or has only recently been completed, knowing that the feedback will be supportive and useful. I have received a great deal of help from people who were further ahead and had more experience than I did. This collection fits with that experience.

Making space for exploration

Kathleen Pithouse-Morgan: The full range of arts-based educational research is still not represented in many of the standard textbooks used by doctoral and early career researchers. The work has a three-decade history, but it is still not consistently present in the places newer researchers go for guidance. This is why we developed The Bloomsbury Handbook of Arts-Based Educational Research (Pithouse-Morgan et al, 2027): to bring together varied approaches and practical examples from different settings.

Arts-based research may not be the path everyone chooses, and that is perfectly fine. However, everyone should have opportunities to experience and explore it, and to engage with both completed research and work in progress. These opportunities should be available to newer researchers wherever they are based.

Charlie Davis: At a time when it can feel like education is becoming increasingly cautious, it is useful to have a space where people can try something less familiar. If you are starting out, it helps to see other people doing this and to recognise that they may not be as far ahead of you as you thought.

Continuing the workshop conversation

Tim Clark: The Newer Researchers workshop invited people to experience object work, poetry, poetic making and storyboarding, and we took part as well. This collection continues that work. It gives newer researchers a presence on the blog and shares examples that others can encounter as part of a community.

Charlie Davis: For me, the blog series embraces the same ethos as the workshop. It makes the work visible, gives people at an early stage a place to contribute and offers a space where those contributions can be received supportively. As our conversation suggests, making arts-based educational research visible means sharing work at different stages and hearing directly from the people doing it. The posts in this series bring together newer researchers who are exploring what creative approaches make possible, while also reflecting openly on the decisions and uncertainties involved.

Their accounts offer several ways into ABER, beginning with Gemma Stafford-Keal, an EdD student at the University of Nottingham and Senior Learning Designer at Nottingham Trent University. She asks how we might make sense of the world through ABER, reflecting on the relationship between making and researching across her life.

Next, Rozana AlBanawi, also an EdD doctoral candidate at the University of Nottingham and founder of Jeddah’s CreativeMornings chapter, explores adult education, personal growth and third spaces. In this post, she shares how working through the “messy middle” of creative participatory research changed her understanding of herself and her role as a researcher.

In the third post, Laura Manison, a Senior Lecturer in Education at the University of the West of England, reflects on the use of ‘poetic playfulness’ in a study exploring the choices of students on a primary initial teacher education programme. Laura reflects on ideas of legitimacy, language and advocacy in relation to ABER.

And in the final post Jayne Hemmins-Dunning, Senior Lecturer at the Northern School of Art, shares learning from the ‘Thursday Afternoon Club’, a doctoral project employing participatory, arts-based, methods with art and design undergraduates. Jayne considers the potential of ABER for empowering students to reflect critically on their personal experiences and reflects on ideas of participation and community in HE research.

We invite you to read the posts and sit with the experiences these newer researchers share. As you do, think about what might help arts-based approaches become more visible, accessible and possible within the higher education spaces of which you are part. Please consider sharing your thoughts by responding to the posts. If you’re attending the SRHE conference in December, have a look for the sessions where colleagues are using creative methods. Together, these exchanges may help us continue learning with and from one another.

Tim Clark is Director of Research and Enterprise for the School of Education and an Associate Professor in Educational Research Practice at the University of the West of England, Bristol. His research focuses on furthering understanding of areas including researcher development, practitioner research, arts-based and narrative methodologies, and research with children and young people.

Charlie Davis is an Associate Professor in Higher Education at the University of Nottingham. He is an experienced researcher who has worked in Higher Education since 2009. Charlie specialises in Arts-based educational research (ABER) approaches as part of participatory co-production of research methodologies. He has extensive experience supervising, mentoring and supporting doctoral students across a range of educational contexts. He is a Senior Fellow of the Higher Education Academy (FHEA) and a co-convenor of the Society for Research into Higher Education (SRHE) Newer Researcher Network.

Kathleen Pithouse-Morgan is Professor of Education at the University of Nottingham and Honorary Professor at the University of KwaZulu-Natal. Her work explores professional learning, self-reflexive scholarship and how the arts can contribute to educational research. She is committed to making arts-based approaches more accessible to researchers, educators and students. Kathleen is grateful to Claudia Mitchell for her many years of mentorship and friendship, and for graciously allowing her contribution to Kathleen’s ABER journey to be acknowledged in this post.

title: Cuadernos político-institucionales
summary:
Novedad editorial

La entrada Cuadernos político-institucionales se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
CLACSO presenta los dos primeros títulos de su Serie Cuadernos Político-Institucionales, la cual recoge los debates estratégicos impulsados por CLACSO y los plasma en documentos de alcance regional que buscan aportar insumos para la incidencia pública y la toma de decisiones en un escenario global atravesado por profundas reconfiguraciones.

El primer cuaderno “Reconfiguraciones geopolíticas y multilateralismo en transformación” reúne distintas perspectivas sobre las reconfiguraciones geopolíticas en curso y abre una pregunta por el lugar de América Latina y el Caribe en un orden internacional en disputa. En un escenario marcado por asimetrías de poder e intereses diversos, examina qué capacidades y formas de articulación necesita construir la región para fortalecer su posición e incidir en la configuración del orden mundial.

El segundo cuaderno “Educación superior en disputa” reúne trabajos que, desde experiencias, disciplinas y territorios diversos, comparten una preocupación por las profundas transformaciones de la educación superior. Estas vuelven a poner en discusión el sentido de la universidad, las formas de producir y compartir conocimiento y su papel en la construcción de sociedades democráticas, igualitarias y justas.

Ambos cuadernos son coordinados por Pablo Vommaro y Nora Goren.

Reconfiguraciones geopolíticas y multilateralismo en transformación. Perspectivas desde el Sur Global

El escenario geopolítico internacional atraviesa una transición abierta. Las jerarquías, instituciones y equilibrios que organizaron las últimas décadas están siendo cuestionados, mientras emergen nuevos actores, polos de poder y espacios de articulación. Pero la transformación del escenario global no conduce por sí misma a un orden más democrático, menos desigual ni más favorable para América Latina y el Caribe.

Este primer Cuaderno Político-Institucional de CLACSO reúne distintas perspectivas para comprender las reconﬁguraciones geopolíticas en curso y, sobre todo, para interrogar el lugar de nuestra región en ellas. Recursos estratégicos, cadenas de valor, ciencia y tecnología, infraestructuras digitales, producción de conocimiento, integración regional y multilateralismo forman hoy parte de una misma disputa por la autonomía. En ese escenario, el desafío es transformar los recursos de la región en capacidades de desarrollo y decisión, aprovechar las oportunidades que abre la multipolaridad y construir una estrategia regional propia frente a la emergencia de nuevos actores internacionales. Es decir, impulsar las capacidades que permitan a América Latina y el Caribe intervenir activamente en la reconﬁguración del escenario geopolítico internacional.

Educación superior en disputa. Entre la mercantilización y la defensa de lo público

La educación superior atraviesa una encrucijada desaﬁante. La desﬁnanciación, la mercantilización de la enseñanza, la ofensiva de las derechas contra el pensamiento crítico y la irrupción de la inteligencia artiﬁcial tensionan el sentido mismo de la universidad y su autonomía.

Este segundo Cuaderno Político-Institucional de CLACSO reúne experiencias y perspectivas de distintos países de la región −de la universidad pública argentina a la experiencia cubana, de Puerto Rico a la universidad comunal de Oaxaca− para comprender las agresiones que enfrenta la educación superior y, sobre todo, para pensar qué universidad queremos construir. En ese escenario, el desafío es fortalecer universidades públicas, autónomas y democráticas, capaces de producir conocimiento común e intervenir en las transformaciones en curso para construir futuros más democráticos e igualitarios.
